{{Short description|Hungarian-born British biochemist (1930–2021)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2025}}
{{eastern name order|Pusztai Árpád}}
'''Árpád János Pusztai''' (8 September 1930 – 17 December 2021<ref>[https://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/254282/pusztai Pusztai]</ref>) was a Hungarian-born British [[biochemist]] and [[nutritionist]] who spent 36 years at the [[Rowett Research Institute]] in [[Aberdeen]], Scotland. He was a world expert on plant [[lectins]], authoring 270 papers and three books on the subject.

In 1998, Árpád Pusztai publicly announced that the results of his research showed feeding [[genetically modified potato]]es to rats had negative effects on their stomach lining and immune system. This led to scientific criticism. Pusztai was suspended and his annual contract was not renewed. The resulting controversy became known as the [[Pusztai affair]].

==Life and career==
Pusztai was born in Budapest, [[Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946)|Hungary]], on 8 September 1930. He was a student of the high school [[Óbudai Árpád Gimnázium]] and later obtained a diploma in chemistry in 1953 from the [[Eötvös Loránd University]] in Budapest. He worked for three years as an associate scientist at the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] before the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956|Hungarian revolution]] against Soviet control in 1956.<ref name ="Deiseroth2005">{{cite book| author=Dieter Deiseroth, Annegret Falter (Hrsg.) |title=Whistleblower in Gentechnik und Rüstungsforschung Preisverleihung 2005: Theodore A. Postol, Árpád Pusztai  |publisher=VMW |year=2006 |isbn=978-3-8305-1262-2}}</ref> After the failed revolution, Pusztai escaped to a [[refugee camp]] in Austria and from there made his way to England.<ref name="Rowell">{{Cite book |last= Rowell |first= Andrew |title= Don't worry, it's safe to eat: the true story of GM food, BSE, & Foot and Mouth |publisher= Earthscan |year=2003 |isbn= 978-1-85383-932-0}}</ref> He completed his doctorate in [[biochemistry]] at the [[Lister Institute]] in London and continued there with his [[post-doctorate]]. In 1963, he was invited to join the Protein Research Department at the [[Rowett Research Institute]] in [[Aberdeen]], Scotland. Pusztai worked at the Rowett Institute for the next 36 years, predominately studying plant [[lectins]]. During that time, he discovered [[glycoproteins]] in plants, authored over 270 research papers, published 3 books,<ref name="Rowell"/> and was considered an "internationally renowned expert on lectins".<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1177/0162243906293885| last1 = Levidow | first1 = L. | last2 = Murphy | first2 = J. | last3 = Carr | first3 = S. | title = Recasting "Substantial Equivalence":Transatlantic Governance of GM Food | journal = Science, Technology, & Human Values | volume = 32 | pages = 26–64 | year = 2007| s2cid = 550454 | url = http://oro.open.ac.uk/6751/1/LLJMSC_SubstEquiv_STHV_07corr.pdf }}</ref> He was made a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1988 and has received fellowships from the [[Leverhulme Trust]].<ref name ="Deiseroth2005"/> Árpád Pusztai was married to Dr Susan Bardócz, with whom he worked at the Rowett Institute. He had two daughters from his first marriage and a stepson from his marriage to Dr. Bardócz.<ref name = "Randerson">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2008/jan/15/academicexperts.highereducationprofile| title=Árpád Pusztai: Biological Divide – James Randerson interviews biologist Árpád Pusztai |work=The Guardian|date=15 January 2008 | location=London | access-date=25 April 2010}}</ref> He died at his home in Aberdeen on 17 December 2021, at the age of 91.<ref>{{cite news |title=PUSZTAI, Dr Arpad FRSE |url=https://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/254282/pusztai |access-date=29 December 2021 |work=The Times |date=29 December 2021}}</ref>

==Pusztai affair==
{{main|Pusztai affair}}
In 1995, Pusztai began research on [[genetic engineering|genetically modified]] potatoes containing the GNA [[lectin]] gene from the [[snowdrop]] plant.<ref name="Rowell"/> His research team fed raw and cooked genetically modified potatoes to rats, using [[desiree potato|Desiree Red]] potatoes as [[Scientific control|controls]]. In 1998, Pusztai said in an interview on a [[World in Action]] programme that his group had observed damage to the intestines and immune systems of rats fed the genetically modified potatoes. He also said,  "If I had the choice, I would certainly not eat it," and "I find it's very unfair to use our fellow citizens as guinea pigs."<ref name = "Randerson"/>

This resulted in a [[media frenzy]], and the director of the Rowett Institute, Philip James, after initially supporting Pusztai, suspended him and banned both him and Susan Bardocz from speaking publicly. He also used misconduct procedures to seize the raw data.<ref name = "Randerson"/> The Rowett Institute eventually published an audit criticizing Pusztai's results<ref>Bourne, F.J., et al (1998) [http://www.rowett.ac.uk/press/OVERVIEW.html Audit Report Overview] Rowett Research Institute, 28 October 1998, Retrieved 28 November 2010 {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205040855/http://www.rowett.ac.uk/press/OVERVIEW.html |date=5 February 2010 }}</ref> and sent the raw data to six anonymous reviewers, who also criticized Pusztai's work.<ref>Bowden, Rebecca [http://www.freenetpages.co.uk/hp/A.Pusztai/RoyalSoc/ReportsAndReplies/RS_referee_reports.txt Six referees comments on Pusztai potato data] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120731163541/http://www.freenetpages.co.uk/hp/A.Pusztai/RoyalSoc/ReportsAndReplies/RS_referee_reports.txt |date=31 July 2012 }} e-mail from Royal Society to Pusztai, 10 May 1999, Retrieved 28 November 2010</ref><ref>Murray, Noreen et al, (1999) [http://www.pages.drexel.edu/~ls39/peer_review/ewen.pdf Review of data on possible toxicity of GM potatoes] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211119142934/http://www.pages.drexel.edu/~ls39/peer_review/ewen.pdf |date=19 November 2021 }} The Royal Society, 1 June 1999, Retrieved 28 November 2010</ref> Pusztai sent the audit report and his rebuttal to scientists who requested it, and in February 1999, twenty-one European and American scientists released a memo supporting Pusztai.<ref name=Enserink1999A>{{cite journal  | author = Enserink, M. | title = BIOENGINEERING: Preliminary Data Touch Off Genetic Food Fight | year = 1999 | journal = Science | pages = 1094–5 | volume = 283 | issue = 5405 | pmid = 10075564  | doi = 10.1126/science.283.5405.1094| bibcode = 1999Sci...283.1094. | s2cid = 8268328 }}</ref>

James and the Rowett Institute released a statement on 10 August falsely accusing Pusztai of using a lectin (Concanavalin A) that was a known toxin. This wasn't true. Pusztai had used the snowdrop lectin, but a gag order prevented him from defending himself publicly until 1999.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rampton, Sheldon |first=Stauber, John |title=Trust Us, We're Experts! |publisher=Jeremy P. Tarcher |year=2001 |isbn=1585421391 |location=New York |pages=152–160}}</ref>

Pusztai's experiment was eventually published as a letter in ''[[The Lancet]]'' in 1999.<ref name="Lancet">{{cite journal |author=Ewen SW, Pusztai A |title=Effect of diets containing genetically modified potatoes expressing Galanthus nivalis lectin on rat small intestine |journal=Lancet |volume=354 |issue=9187 |pages=1353–4 |date=October 1999 |pmid=10533866 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(98)05860-7 |s2cid=17252112 }}</ref> Because of the controversial nature of his research, the letter was reviewed by six reviewers – three times the usual number. One publicly opposed the letter, another thought it was flawed, but wanted it published "to avoid suspicions of a conspiracy against Pusztai and to give colleagues a chance to see the data for themselves," while the other four raised questions that were addressed by the authors.<ref name=Enserink1999B>{{cite journal | last1 = Enserink | first1 = Martin | year = 1999 | title = The Lancet Scolded Over Pusztai Paper | journal = Science | volume = 286 | issue = 5440| pages = 656a–656 | doi = 10.1126/science.286.5440.656a | pmid=10577214| s2cid = 153199625 }}</ref> The letter reported [[Statistical significance|significant]] differences between the thickness of the gut [[epithelium]] of rats fed genetically modified potatoes and of rats fed the control diet.<ref name="Lancet"/>

The [[Royal Society of Medicine]] declared that the study 'is flawed in many aspects of design, execution and analysis' and that 'no conclusions should be drawn from it'.<ref name=key>{{cite journal | last1 = Key | first1 = Suzie | last2 = Julian | last3 = Ma | first3 = K-C | last4 = Drake | first4 = Pascal MW | year = 2008 | title = Genetically modified plants and human health | journal = Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine | volume = 101 | issue = 6| pages = 290–298 | doi = 10.1258/jrsm.2008.070372 | pmc=2408621 | pmid=18515776}}</ref> For example, too few rats per test group were used to derive meaningful, statistically significant data.<ref name=key/>

He was one of several scientists interviewed in the 2010 documentary [[Scientists Under Attack: Genetic Engineering in the Magnetic Field of Money]] who, based on their findings, have criticized the use of genetic modification for food.

==Aftermath==
Pusztai's annual contract at Rowett was not renewed following the incident and he moved back to Hungary. He gave lectures on his GE potato work and on claimed dangers in general of genetic engineering of crop plants.<ref>[http://www.cielap.org/pdf/ArpadPusztai.pdf The Canadian Institute for Environmental Law and Policy]</ref> In 2005, he received the [[Whistleblower]] Award of the [[Federation of German Scientists]] and the German section of the International Association of Lawyers against Nuclear Arms (IALANA).<ref name ="Deiseroth2005"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbd.int/doc/external/mop-04/fgs-1-en.pdf|title=Federation of German Scientists}}</ref> In 2009, Pusztai and his wife, Prof. Bardócz Zsuzsa, received the [[Stuttgart Peace Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.die-anstifter.de/?p=3385|title=Stuttgarter Friedenspreis 2009: Prof. Dr. Arpad Pusztai|date=23 December 2009 |accessdate=10 February 2011|language=German}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Global to local: Stuttgart Peace Prize honors GMO whistleblowers|date=December 2009|author=NJ Jaeger|newspaper=LA Examiner}}</ref>
